prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. The case for dropping it is not foolish, and it deserves a fair hearing, but it rests on a picture of childhood learning that is too narrow. It treats handwriting as a transcription technology that keyboards have now superseded, when for a seven-year-old it is something closer to a training ground for the hand, the eye and the mind together. Joined-up writing, taught well and early, is the most efficient form of that training we have, and abandoning it would cost more than it saves.

Start with the argument against, because it is stronger than its critics admit. Most adult writing now happens on screens. Children will sit exams on laptops, apply for jobs through web forms and send messages with their thumbs. Teaching time is finite, and every lesson spent on looping letter exits is a lesson not spent on spelling, grammar, reading or coding. Some countries have already moved in this direction, with Finland and parts of the United States making keyboard instruction a larger part of the early curriculum. Add that many adults abandon cursive the moment they leave school, settling into a hybrid scrawl of print and joins, and the sceptic asks a reasonable question. If nobody keeps the skill, why force it on everyone?

The answer begins with what the adult scrawl actually shows. Those adults did not invent fluent handwriting from nothing. They built their personal hand on top of a taught foundation, and the hybrid they ended up with is fast precisely because it borrowed the economy of joined letters where it helped. People who never learned any joined writing tend to write in slow, effortful print. Speed matters here for a reason beyond convenience. A child who must think hard about forming each letter has less mental capacity left for what the sentence should say. Handwriting that has become automatic frees working memory for composition, and research on early writing has repeatedly found that fluency in letter formation is linked to the length and quality of what young children produce. A fluent joined hand is one of the quickest routes to that automaticity, because the pen stays on the page, the movement flows from letter to letter, and the child learns words as continuous motions rather than as piles of separate marks.

That last point is where cursive earns its place most clearly. In print, every letter begins and ends with a lift, and each lift is a small decision about where the next letter goes. Joined writing removes many of those decisions. The word becomes a single gesture with a rhythm, and rhythm is how the body remembers things. Teachers of spelling have long observed that children who write common patterns as joined units, the ing at the end of a word, the tion, the double letters, tend to absorb them as units too. The hand learns the shape of the word, and the spelling comes with it. A keyboard cannot offer the same thing. Every letter on a keyboard is the same small press of the same small key, so the kinaesthetic difference between typing a word correctly and typing it wrongly is almost nothing. The finger does not feel the error.

There is also the matter of what handwriting does to the thinking that goes on while it happens. Studies comparing note-taking by hand with note-taking on laptops have suggested that writing by hand pushes students to summarise and rephrase, because they cannot keep pace with a speaker word for word, while typists tend to transcribe. The findings are not beyond dispute, and some replications have been weaker than the original claim, so it would be foolish to lean on them too hard. But work on young children points in a consistent direction. Brain imaging studies have found that preliterate children who practise forming letters by hand show stronger activation in reading-related regions than those who type or trace the same letters. The movement of making a letter seems to help the child recognise it. If handwriting supports learning to read, then it is not a rival to literacy teaching. It is part of it.

A second argument concerns children who struggle. It is sometimes said that cursive is hard on them, and that print is kinder to those with dyslexia or poor motor control. The truth is more interesting. Many specialists who work with dyslexic pupils recommend joined writing, and some do so because it removes a particular failure that print invites, the reversal of letters such as b and d. In a joined script, the starting point of each letter is fixed on the baseline, so b and d are formed in different ways and are much harder to confuse. A continuous line also reduces the spacing problems that make a child's writing a jumble of loose letters. None of this is a universal cure, and a child with severe motor difficulties will need adapted support, including a keyboard. But that is an argument for provision at the margins, not for withdrawing the default from everyone. We do not abolish swimming lessons because some children cannot swim without aids.

The practical objection is time, and here the sceptics are simply wrong about the numbers. Teaching joined writing does not require a large block of the day. It requires short, regular, well-taught practice, ten or fifteen minutes at a time, in the years when children are already learning to form letters. The marginal cost of teaching letters in a joined style rather than in print is small if it is done from the start, and it is highest precisely when schools treat it as an afterthought, bolting it onto Year 3 after children have spent two years building habits that must then be unlearned. The sensible policy is not to add cursive on top of print but to teach one consistent, simple joined style, with no decorative loops and exit strokes only where they help, from the first year. Many schools already do this successfully.

Some will say that the real cost is not time but opportunity, that the hours would be better spent on typing. But the two are not in competition. Children can and should learn to type, and the best moment is later, from around the age of eight or nine, once the hand has learned what a letter is. Touch typing is a skill that rewards direct instruction and practice at an age when the fingers are strong enough to do it properly. Nothing about teaching joined handwriting in the early years prevents that, and the two skills serve different purposes. One is a tool for thinking and learning at a desk with a pencil. The other is a tool for producing text quickly at a screen. A literate adult needs both, and a school that teaches only one has made a choice about what kind of writer it wants to produce.

There is, finally, an argument that is harder to quantify but still real. Handwriting is the way most children first meet writing as a personal act. A child's hand is recognisably theirs, and learning to make it fluent and legible is one of the earliest experiences of mastering a craft through repetition. A signature, a birthday card, a note left on the kitchen table, a shopping list, an exam answer in a hall where laptops are forbidden: these are all still part of ordinary life, and they will remain so for decades. A person who cannot read joined writing is also cut off from a great deal of the written record, from a grandparent's letters to the archives of their own country. Reading cursive takes far less effort if one has learned to write it, and it would be an odd generation that could read a thousand years of print but not the handwritten letter in the attic.

None of this means the old ways should be defended for their own sake. The Victorian copybook, with its rows of identical flourishes and its penalties for blots, is not worth reviving, and a school that polices the exact slant of a child's letters is wasting everybody's time. The goal is fluent, legible, reasonably fast writing, and a child who reaches it with a slightly idiosyncratic style has succeeded. What matters is that the school gives every child a real chance to get there, and joined-up writing, simply taught and sensibly timed, remains the most reliable route we know.

So the question is not whether handwriting is still relevant in a digital age. It is whether we want children to meet writing first as a movement of the hand that they come to own, or as a series of identical keystrokes. The evidence, modest as parts of it are, favours the hand. The costs are small, the benefits to reading, spelling and fluency are plausible and consistent, and the loss, once a generation stops learning, would be hard to reverse. Primary schools should go on teaching joined-up handwriting, and teach it better than many of them do now.
